newsitem.title: SWEDEN: INSTANT VIEW - Analysts views on Swedish CPI data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Analysts views on Swedish CPI data.

text.p: Sweden's central statistics bureau on Tuesday said the consumer price index fell in December by 0.2 percent to give the third consecutive month of a year-on-year negative inflation trend.
TOMAS NIEMELA, ECONOMIST, ARAGON:
"For the most part as expected. It's still low interest rate costs that are pulling the figure. The figures are still good, and we are now seeing the bottom."
BJORN ENGLUND, ANALYST, UNIBANK MARKETS:
"I don't think it was anything especially overwhelming. It was in line with expectations.

The after Christmas sales have affected prices somewhat. We have now seen the bottom of CPI. From, and starting in January, we will see an increase with a year-on-year rise in January of 0.2 to 0.3 percent."
OLLE DJERF, ECONOMIST, NORDBANKEN :
"It seems as if we reached bottom in November 1996. But the rate of inflation will be very low during the first months of the year and there could be additional negative figures.
Still, it is likely that we will see positive figures ahead with an increasing curve during the autumn because interest rates will not fall."
SVEN-ARNE SVENSSON, ECONOMIST, HAGSTROMER & QVIBERG :
"The January figure is definitely going to be below the Riksbank's target of around 0.5 to one percent.
We still have the world's lowest inflation rate, but this is among those few months when it was actually higher than expected.
I don't think this will affect the Riksbank's decision about rate cuts.
(The Riksbank) will maybe wait until Thursday and cut both the corridor and the rate then."
KATHARINA HOYLAND, ECONOMIST, J P MORGAN:
"It is a little higher than expected. It probably is because of higher energy prices, but ... there is probably no inflationary pressure on core prices yet.
The Riksbank may choose to see more details before they decide to cut the repo rate if they have not already decided to do so."
JAMES MCKAY, ECONOMIST, PAINE WEBBER:
"The figure is mainly related to oil prices, which have gone up lately. I think we are at the bottom of the inflationary cycle, but I don't think any inflationary pressure is going to develop.
I think that Swedish interest rates will come down to German levels, especially if progress is made with the wage negotiations."
